title: Backcasting: Evaluator Diversity as a Requirement for Manipulation-Resistant Assessment
original_idea: Construct a small ensemble of diverse deception detectors (behavioral probe, activation probe, stylometric classifier, human evaluator). Test whether the ensemble achieves lower false negative rates than any individual detector.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: If evaluator diversity is structurally necessary for reliable detection, this is a fundamental design principle for safety evaluation. Clear impact on evaluation system architecture.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building four different detection methods (behavioral probe, activation probe, stylometric classifier, human evaluation) each requires its own implementation. Activation probes require interpretability tools. The ensemble approach is conceptually simple but implementation is complex.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Four detection methods plus ensemble evaluation is effectively four mini-projects. Even simplified versions of each method require separate implementation and calibration. Well beyond 30hrs.

novelty.reasoning: While individual detection methods (behavioral probes, activation probes, stylometric classifiers) have been studied separately, and multimodal deception detection challenges exist (SVC 2025, DecepBench), no published work specifically constructs an ensemble of diverse AI deception detectors and measures whether the ensemble achieves lower false negative rates than individual detectors for AI scheming detection. The closest work discusses combining confessions and probes as a 'model honesty stack' but nobody has wired these into a single pipeline and measured combined detection rates. The ensemble-for-AI-deception angle is mostly novel.
